utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Regrettably Judge Chowhan is unwell this morning, but having considered the position we think it best to continue in the interests of justice and in everyone concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That last passage was in the interests of everyone concerned. Good morning, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination by Mr. Ivetic will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the outset of your evidence on Friday continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Deretic. Last Friday I believe we left off after you had just told us about the various radio relays that were in place upon which the Serbian MUP's radio communications were based and you told us about the relay Goles being struck several days before the Pristina SUP building was struck by NATO. If you could tell us the second part of my question which looking at the transcript I did not get answered, what was the immediate effect of the NATO strike against the Goles radio relay as far as the radio communications and telephone communications of the Serbian MUP are concerned on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ivetic. As for your question, I can say that Goles was a very important centre or node, not only from the point of view of the needs of the ministry and the communications of the ministry, but also the entire telecommunications system that existed in Kosovo and Metohija, that is to say that this was important from the point of view of radio, television, and broadcasting TV and radio programmes from the point of view of Telekom and the Telekom transmission system and also from the point of view of the needs of the MUP and the Army of Yugoslavia. What I know is the Telekom had its own radio relay node up at Goles where transmission systems were organized towards the Metohija part of Kosovo and Metohija and the Kosovo Pomoravlje. When the transmission facilities at Goles were destroyed, it became impossible to have any kind of communication towards the Pec area, Djakovica and Prizren areas, and also Gnjilane. When I'm referring to these towns I'm referring to their surrounding areas as well. Of course, the radio communications of the ministry were also in that part that was covered by this locality and they were rendered ineffective. So the damage was large-scale. I think that even before the bombing of the SUP of Pristina took place Goles was bombed, and I know that it was Goles this was bombed Mokra Gora and Stari Trg and sometime after that the SUP in Pristina; however, I don't have these exact documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could ask you to clarify, you said with respect to radio communications that the communications of the ministry were also in that part that was covered by this locality and they were rendered ineffective. Which locality or which municipalities radio communications were affected or terminated by the strike on the Goles radio relay?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to explain that by destroying the Telekom transmission system, Telekom is the only land-line operator in Serbia, I think that's a well-known fact, isn't it, but the telephone and telegraph links, the entire system, the special telephone system and the dispatch transmission system was organized in the following way: Telekom transmission systems were used, so when they were destroyed there was no longer any possibility to have dispatches sent to these towns and areas that I mentioned a few moments ago. Also, telephone lines were dead, especially when soon after that the SUP building was hit. Then this was rendered impossible too. There were several repeaters that were used by the MUP covering part of the territory of Pristina, the road from Pristina to Urosevac, part of the road towards Pec, and that would be about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you know how many times Goles was struck by NATO forces and were any of the other repeaters that you testified about on Friday, radio relays on other locations that you testified about on Friday, also the targets of NATO air-strikes during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the exact records on this, how many times each and every facility was hit, but I do know that during these strikes these locations were constant targets. I said a moment ago that Mokra Gora, Goles, and Stari Trg had been hit. This was sometimes in the second -- sometime in the second half of March. Already in the beginning of April all these other facilities were systematically destroyed, one after the other: Butovacki Breg, Mokra Gora, Cabrat, Cviljen. So in the first half of April all the facilities were destroyed, although many of them had been destroyed every time there were NATO air-strikes they were hit yet again. So it's not only that the construction infrastructure was destroyed, it wasn't only the pillars and the actual facilities, but it was the entire infrastructure that was destroyed, the transmission lines with the transformer stations, the reserve feed systems, roads, waterworks. Quite simply, there were several locations that were dead and that was a dead location. If I may add one more thing, up to the present day most of these facilities had not been renovated, which means that the damage was enormous and to this very day this affects the development of Serbian telecommunications in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now could you tell us -- we've previously had evidence in this case about the NATO bombings of the Telekom building in the centre of Pristina. Can you tell us a little bit about this and its effect on the communications system used by the Serbian Ministry of the Interior among others?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Telekom building in Pristina, telecommunications centre 2, as it was called, is in the immediate vicinity of the provincial Executive Council building. It was the very heart of these transmission systems that Telekom had organized for the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. That is to say that in this building that is where all the communications within Kosovo ended and then -- it worked both ways, from those places to Pristina and vice versa. As these facilities were destroyed, because we said a few moments ago that Goles caused an interruption of links to Kosovo Pomoravlje and Metohija, so there was only Urosevac and Mitrovica left where some kind of public communication could take place including our own, the MUP communication. However, when this facility was destroyed, this possibility ceased as well, totally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you've talked about the attacks on the SUP building, the radio relays, and the Telekom building. After that, what form of communications was still available after those specific attacks for the Serbian Ministry of the Interior located in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should say that from Pristina to the other part of Serbia there was still the possibility of affecting some communications via optic cables and systems that were carried through via that optic cable. Pristina, Nis, and further on towards the rest of Serbia. As for the communication between Pristina and other places within the province, there was no longer any possibility of organizing any communications systems there, those that the ministry could use for its own communications. In a word, the only communication that was possible was via messenger, courier, although that was unsafe too since there were air-strikes all the time and there were attacks by Albanian terrorists. So it wasn't that simple for couriers to reach Pristina from all these other places; however, this was not within my line of work, the organization of courier messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you've mentioned this optical cable. Did that continue to be in existence throughout the war or was that affected at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these optical cables that exist, as I've already said, made it possible for there to be communications between Pristina and the other parts of Serbia; however, there weren't optical cables from Pristina to other places in Kosovo and Metohija. This cable was hit on one occasion, too, so even that was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's take a moment to talk about the one instance where the optical cable was bombed by NATO. Did you have occasion to be an eye-witness to the after effects of that strike?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I received the information on this misfortune, together with the technical director of Telekom in Pristina, I went very soon after this happened to the actual site with the intention of carrying out an on-site investigation and analysis of the damages so that we would deal with them and repair things as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you where this bombing of the optical cable took place and if there were any civilian casualties as a result of this NATO attack?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This took place at the bridge near Luzane, that is to say the bus travelling from Nis to Pristina full of passengers was hit on that bridge and the bridge was hit as well as this installation, the optical cable that went under the bridge. That's quite simply the way Telekom places its cables.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the record and for information of the Trial Chamber, we'll be submitting a document later. I don't think we have a translation at present, 6D998, a report of the on-scene investigation conducted after this NATO strike, which hit a civilian bus, the Nis Express, on the bridge in the village of Luzane, 1 May 1999; and this report gives details about the attack and about the civilian casualties, both ethnic Serb and ethnic Albanian that were on this bus going from Pristina to Nis. Once we have that translation, we'll submit from the bar table the documents so that we don't have to go through all the gory details with this witness who came to the scene after the fact -- after the attack but before all the civilian casualties had been assisted by the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can move to another area, sir. Following the bombing of the SUP building in Pristina, how often did the MUP staff and the secretariat of interior in Pristina have to relocate during the course of the continued NATO war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the locations used by the SUP of Pristina and the staff -- well, there were several of them, there were several locations that the staff was at, and at the same time every day, or rather, every other day they would change their location. Also, many organizational units of the Pristina SUP behaved in a similar way because the fear from bombing was great, the precision of NATO bombs that were hitting certain locations within towns were depressing, if I can put it that way. It is with high precision that they could hit any facility. The answer is that these locations often changed where these organizational units were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with regards to the relocation sites that were utilised by the MUP staff and with regards to the technology and communications that were available at those locations, was there any parity or comparison to the level of communications during peacetime in regards to communications with the terrain?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, this question is really not a serious one, is it? A few moments ago we were talking about the terrible devastation that took place over all the telecommunications systems. So really, I mean, the answer can be that it was only the most basic telephone communications that could be introduced and only in those parts of town where they still existed. When the Telekom system that existed it was the telephone exchange that was also destroyed, the only telephone exchange that existed in the city of Pristina. By virtue of that fact, most of the city of Pristina that was covered by this telephone exchange could not have any kind of telephone communications because the cable lines were also destroyed that ended up at the end users. So what we could do from the communications department was to have one or two telephone numbers that we would organize for each and every location where the MUP staff and the organizational units were at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last area I'd like to ask you about relates to Exhibit P1052, a document which has been used by the Prosecution in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have a hard copy which I would like to have the usher's assistance to give to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this document is entitled as a plan of radio communications. Can you tell me looking at this document first of all whether this document originates from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia or not? Is this form a form used by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is certainly not a facility of the Ministry of the Interior because, first of all, MUP does not write "military secrets" on its documents, right? It says "strictly confidential" but not "military secret." And also, I don't know who did the designation of units of the Ministry of the Interior. They are not designated was in the proper way. I'm also not aware of the call-sign Pastrik and also this participant, Joint Command, I don't know who that is. Also this way of marking the frequencies is not one that exists in the Ministry of the Interior, so at this point in time I really don't understand how these links between the organizational units of the MUP and these other users could be organized.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could ask you to focus on the MUP units that are listed on the first -- on each page, on the document, if you could leaf through the three pages in front of you, and could you tell us are these coded call-signs for these MUP units, are they what are in the business known as 1-, 2-, or 3-digit codings or encryptions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, OD MUP probably means MUP detachment, odred MUP. There are single-digit numbers in every one of these cases, except in this one case where it says the tenth detachment of MUP. So there are a lot of single-digit numbers and only one two-digit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, does this information comport with your recollection and knowledge of the radio call-signs actually utilised by the Serbian MUP in 1998 or 1999, that is to say did the call-signs used by the MUP have single-digit numbers, as are reflected in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, MUP detachments were designated by two-digit or three-digit number, the 21st, the 22nd, the 122nd, the 124th, and so on and so forth. It was never a single-digit number. It was always two- or three-digit numbers. As for the call-signs, we did use Sara, but I have to explain something first, when we were talking about the plan of intentions and using radio telecommunications, we said that according to this plan that is adopted by the state, the MUP and the army use separate frequencies. Since they use separate frequencies, frequency ranges, they can use separate call-signs, although they do not belong to the same units. So I believe that, for example, BG-243.mbr, that that's a mechanised brigade. It says Sara-60. Now, Sara, Sara is the Prizren call-sign of the SUP, that is to say that they used similar call-signs. Then we've got Cegar too. Cegar is something I find familiar. I think that it was used by the Nis detachment of the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Deretic, I thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I conclude my direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. To help me understand your last point, Mr. Deretic, are you saying that because the VJ and the MUP used different frequencies, they also used identical call-signs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that that might have happened. I did not have any insight into this and I don't know what call-signs were used by members of the military; but I do know, for instance, Sara is one of the regular call-signs that was used by SUP Prizren, that is to say the Ministry of the Interior in Prizren. I don't know what call-signs were used by the members of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you have nothing at all to do with communications between the MUP and the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was cooperation there at technical level in the sense of giving technical assistance. Quite simply, I mean the MUP had a trained and equipped team that was involved in the maintenance of repeaters, radio stations, and very often when our colleagues from the technical services from communications we would help them when they would call us. We would help them since there was quite a bit of equipment at the same locations, there was a kind of cooperation there and mutual assistance, too; that is to say that in the field of technical matters in overcoming certain technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you, though, be familiar with the complete list of MUP call-signs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we had extracts -- I spoke during my previous testimony about the rules on the regulation of radio telephone communications in MUP, and that the basic directory of the system is an integral part of those rules. This directory provides all the call-signs for all organizational units of the ministry, and it is only natural that I as a person who was involved in that line of work, I did have this basic directory with all the call-signs of the regular organizational units of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was there no similar directory that you had from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. Those are strictly confidential documents, and they are not given to other users.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic -- sorry, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. A couple questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, good morning. My name is Djuro Cepic, and I'm one of the Defence counsel for General Vladimir Lazarevic, who also used to work in communications. You spoke about separate systems, separate frequency ranges; you mentioned also the locations of Butovacki Breg, Stari Trg, and Mokra Gora and you said they were repeatedly destroyed during air-strikes. Are you aware that there existed on those locations also military antennas, military transmission systems?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that because those were so-called stationary hubs of communications that the Army of Yugoslavia used in organizing their communications for command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that they were repeatedly destroyed during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Speaking of the call-signs and you said that MUP had a separate document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call into e-court 5D1427, please. Unfortunately, we still don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deretic, will you please read this. What is this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Temporary directory of the user of radio relay communications Jablanica" -- sorry, "radio telephone communications."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Who issued the document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you already said on page 114 on Friday, what about regular channels? Please read the first three.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the regular channels? Well, in the first column on the left we see secretariats of internal affairs of Kosovo and Metohija; the middle column are the channels used in VHF; and in the third column are call-signs that the secretariats used within their regional networks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Read the first two.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SUP Pristina is at 58 VHF, very high frequency, and I used that term, regional channel. So through this channel, 58, Pristina had audibility and communications with its own departments of internal affairs. The general call-sign of all members of radio communications within SUP Pristina is Sitnica, of course with this general call-sign in keeping with the numbering system there goes a one-digit, two-digit, or three-digit numbers, and it can be extended to five digits. The same applies to all secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And read the second one to know the call-sign.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SUP Kosovska Mitrovica. Can you please scroll up. Thank you. SUP Kosovska Mitrovica, regular channel 52, organized in very high frequency, VHF, the call-sign of all members of the secretariat of internal affairs in Kosovska Mitrovica is Ibar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mention has been made of this name, Sara, can you explain for what frequency range it was used?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SUP Prizren used the 46th channel in VHF, and the call-sign for its users Sara. So within a similar system in keeping with the rules of use of radio telecommunications a one, two, or three-digit number is added to this call-sign Sara.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And that has nothing to do with the army or its frequencies?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you been recorded correctly as saying a one- two- or three-digit number is added to this call-sign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did say that. For instance, the chief of SUP Pristina is Sitnica 1. Most of the other users have three-digit numbers. In some cases a two-digit number is possible in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Earlier you said something to us about there being no one-digit numbers. What did that relate to? You said MUP detachments were designated by two-digit or three-digit numbers. That's a different situation, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another situation, for instance, is the name of the detachment. You don't have the 1st Detachment of the PJP or the 2nd Detachment; there is 121st Detachment or the 21st, that's why I said the units of the MUP don't have one-digit numbers of units. This is something different. This has to do with call-signs and radio traffic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please look, Mr. Deretic, at the bottom of the page and read to us this subheading.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Coded locations."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Read a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 0 Duge Njive, 7 Kraljane, 8 Jablanica -- 18 Rznic, 32 -- sorry, 33 Volujak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These numbers, numbered signs, in dispatches and communications should indicate these geographic locations?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know about that, but it all depends on the way of transmission of certain information. It's possible. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is the heading here?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Coded call-signs, code tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Read these headings that you see in bold and pick a number.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subheadings are green, red, yellow, blue, white, grey, each has one column below, and they contain codes for a certain situation that a unit might find itself in. I said something about this on Friday. This way of coding information, this list that contains combined codes, combining colour and number, in view of the situation in our traffic, frequent jamming and problems, this was used for a purpose. 0 combined with a certain colour says we have people wounded; red 2, we are expecting an attack; those are normal codes that I used even in many regular actions. I as chief of administration within the base of the ministry - and we are talking about the period after 2001, when we were organizing security for football matches and similar actions - we used signs like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This whole document and all these codes were only for the use of the MUP, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. Can I just see the previous page again?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could just assist for a second, this temporary directory is available with a translation at P1071.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This page, where the users are indicated. SAJ is an organizational unit of the ministry. I don't know which of the users in sector 2 or sector 1 it could be, I don't recognise this because I haven't seen this document until now. Bozur, for instance, is a call-sign very frequently used by police units. I suppose that this must be one of the police units, Manir 1 and Manir 2 is not familiar, but it looks like a format that the administration for communications defines when such security-related actions are to be put in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deretic, did MUP have its own encryption system?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The encryption system was within the purview of the state security sector, and if we talk about dispatches sent from Pristina within that unified system at the level of the ministry that was organized for transmitting dispatches, the public security sector transmitted dispatches with a lower degree of confidentiality and are not, therefore, encrypted; they go openly. Transmission of encrypted dispatches was within the purview of the state security sector and the services in the state security sector that were in charge of that, because the public security sector did not have the appropriate equipment to send that kind of dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deretic, would I be right if I said that you had not seen a single dispatch in your practice sent to the Army of Yugoslavia or by the Army of Yugoslavia to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I? Of course I did not. A dispatch with any degree of confidentiality is handed directly to the person to whom it is addressed, nobody else has the right to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the communication between the army and the police did not go by way of dispatches?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it did. I think that in the organization of the telegraph system the army did not have a connection to that system. It must have been effected through letters, correspondence, not dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the use of the telephone network that relied on the Telekom. Was it the case that a garrison commander trying to communicate with the chief of SUP would use that kind of telephone network?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it wasn't quite clear. Could you rephrase the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The telephone network used by the MUP or the regular telephone lines, is that something that a garrison commander in some town would use trying to communicate with the chief of SUP somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the users of this network of the MUP were users who were members of the Army of Yugoslavia -- the MUP of Yugoslavia, that is, and such communication would need to have approval of the administration for communications. On request, the competent administration would have to approve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. Could we call 5D2 -- that is, 218, 5D218.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about the illegal radio station Free Kosovo. This is a report from the command of the Pristina Corps. Would you look at 1.2, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It's a document from end April 1999. Yes, go on, read it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "The illegal radio station Free Kosovo continues to broadcast lies about the successes of the so-called KLA in clashes with the Army of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This document is from late April 1999. Do you know maybe that throughout the whole war period practically the radio -- this particular radio station broadcast its programme?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke on Friday about colleagues from the telecommunications ministry whose work or duty it was to locate the precise location of this radio station. From what I know, they never managed to do this, and the reason was that the radio station that called itself Slobodna Kosovo, free Kosovo, and broadcast a programme, we heard about what sort of a programme, was a mobile station, it kept constantly changing its broadcast location. I know this because I talked with representatives of those services from the ministry for telecommunications. It was not stationary, the facility, it was mounted on a vehicle and quickly changed its location. The locations were not just a few kilometres apart, but they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You told us all this on Friday. Could you just answer the question, please. Do you know whether throughout the war this station continued to broadcast, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if it was throughout the whole war, but I know that it was never pin-pointed, so probably yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Deretic, thank you. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Deretic, I'm sorry to go back to what I asked you about before, but I remain unclear about this. When you were dealing with the numbers of the detachments of the MUP, which I understand are all either double- or triple-digit numbers, are you saying that a call-sign for the detachment of the MUP must have double or triple digits in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The call-sign -- actually, I wasn't calling about the PJP detachment call-signs, but just the insignia or the markings of the detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem is that the matter was raised in the context of call-signs. Now, it may be Mr. Ivetic will want to re-examine on that and clarify, but I certainly am unclear about the point now. I understand you simply to be referring to the actual designation number of the individual PJP detachment. You will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Deretic. Did you hold any rank in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the technical services for a while were not treated as authorised officials, so they had so-called post names. So in 2001 sometime we also received ranks so that in 2005 these ranks were abolished at the ministry and for all the other organizational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So did you have a rank in 2001 until 2005 but at no other time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999, did you wear a uniform to work or did you wear civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us that --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Prosecutor. At the time that I had a rank I also wore civilian clothes. I wore civilian clothes throughout the whole time. I didn't have any kind of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that from the 1st of June, 1999, you became a member of the MUP staff. Is it correct that prior to that 1st of June, 1999, you were never a member of the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, until the 1st of June, 1999, up until then I was never a member of the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In June of 1998 we've seen a document from Minister Stojiljkovic appointing a staff, which included a Captain Cankovic to be the assistant head for communications. Did you take his place in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From mid-1998 and 1999, he was chief of communications at the staff, and then from the 1st of June, 1999, it was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ivetic, I think, on Friday had asked you about whether or not you had seen a document signed by General Djordjevic naming you as a member of the joint -- of the MUP staff. Do you recall having seen that document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the document that was shown to me for the first time during the proofing from my testimony -- actually, I never saw it before that, that's the document that refers to me as the assistant or the chief of communications for wire systems. Are you talking about that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, and you told us you had never seen that before you came here or you were preparing to testify, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see the document which is Exhibit P1505 from the 16th of June, 1998, which is Minister Stojiljkovic's decision creating a MUP staff? Did you see that one during your preparations?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, to save time, I'll indicate to you that that decision in its text makes reference to the specific document in which you had been named by General Djordjevic in 1998 as assistant head of staff for wire communications; and the minister's document says it supersedes that one in which you were named. Would you agree with me that that may be one reason you never saw it, because it got superseded by the minister's other, later order?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's how it was. The first decision referring to me as the chief of communications is something that I never received. It was not given to me. I assume that the other members who were mentioned in the same decision did not receive the decision either. For me, this was a completely unknown document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, on Friday in one of your answers you were talking about the period before the bombing when police units in carrying out actions worked with hand-held radios. And you mentioned that these were only good up to a couple of kilometres, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You went on in that answer to say that from Pristina such communications could not be monitored, that Pristina could perhaps receive information if the detachment commander possibly from some location used a call station to call a radio user in Pristina. Can you explain that for me? What's a call station?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a call station, but it's actually a mobile, a mounted, station. Kolska Stanica is a radio station that is installed or mounted on a vehicle and that is where this name comes from, it's a mounted station. So this station can broadcast with a stronger frequency, 10, 15, 20 watts, so it has a larger range than the hand-held station because the hand-held station is of 3 or 2 watts, exceptionally it can be of 5 watts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, this station is mounted on a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All official vehicles of the ministry or most of them, not all of them, I can't say that, have radios installed, especially the patrol vehicles. They have to have such stations, radios, installed, the patrol police, those vehicles that are clearly marked as police vehicles at that time all had radios in the vehicles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I realize it depends on weather conditions and terrain, but generally what was the range for those radios?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The station range is something that is relative. In order to explain that, I would have to go back to the frequencies, the range, the way radio waves spread in the particular frequency. The dominant wave is the direct wave, so for a radio communication to be achieved there must be optical visibility between the receiver and the transmitter antennas. In case such a radio signal encounters an obstacle, it reflects off it, and you can be relatively close, but if you have a hill between two users, you would not be able to hear each other. You can be farther away, but if the configuration is such that it is a flat terrain without elevations, without hills, then you can have communications. So it's a few kilometres in the simplex method of operations when two stations are working in a local area, and it would be more or less the manner of operation that police members used in the field, the simplex method of operation using hand-held radios.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And under optimal conditions at the highest point for kilometres around do you know what the effective range would be, with no obstacles in between?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This depends on the power of the hand-held radio, let's say 3 or 4 kilometres using the simplex method.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe I got confused, but the mobile mounted radio station, that's -- is that a hand-held radio that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hand-held radios are called transmission ones; vehicle-mounted stationed are called mobile stations -- the hand-held radios are called portable radios, portable because they can be carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what I've been trying to find out about is the range on the mobile radios. Is that what we've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mobile, the mounted stations, it's the same case, the terrain configuration had a significant effect on the quality of the communication and no one can say for sure if it's 2 kilometres, 3, or 5. It's simply something that has to do with the wave, the magnetic waves are disseminated, the way they are carried and the type of the radio waves also.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The reason I started asking this was because you said Pristina could perhaps receive information if the detachment commander possibly from some location used a call station to call a radio user in Pristina, and I got the impression that meant the detachment commander could be in contact with Pristina at some distance greater than 5 kilometres. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible. Only in that case then you use the semi-duplex manner of operation. The whole time we were talking about repeater devices and transmission locations, there were repeater devices at these transmission locations, which enabled communications at a larger distance. We were talking about radio networks and that we can secure radio communications of the secretariat seat with the departments of the SUPs and the Ministry of Internal Affairs branches. So in that case, the staff could possibly communicate with them if the territory was well covered by radio signals; if it wasn't, then they would have to do their best and find a means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think I became confused when you were talking about simplex versus duplex or semi-duplex mode. Let me move on to something else. At page 119 and 120 on Friday's transcript you mentioned that MUP is not intended for war situations, and for that reason the concept of our system of communication was such that the equipment was intended for stationary conditions of work. And then you went on to say: "So looking at it in that way, the MUP did not have the equipment that was intended for wartime action or operation." But in the MUP you must have had some sort of contingency plan for emergencies or natural disasters or even war or rebellion, right, some back-up plan in case your primary or stationary communications were disabled or disrupted, et cetera, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our radio systems were operative much before the actual staff came about, and that was the infrastructure, the telecommunications infrastructure that is being made available to members of the police, MUP, and I say this with all authority, did have some equipment for that tactical level for application in special actions. Our equipment was installed and it was ready for use. We didn't depend on any activities, we didn't prepare something new for the police. The radio network was operational and whoever happened to be in a specific territory would use that infrastructure. So in this way we worked in all the ministry organizational units in the entire area of Serbia. That is why I said that the MUP did not have any tactical communications that were meant for wartime use. It was some peacetime configuration, let's put it that way, of radio networks that was also used in wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So when the war actually started and your primary communications systems were destroyed and damaged, as you described, what methods did you use to try and make up for this lack of capability?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The radio stations were used, but they were used in local works -- work in 2-kilometre range. So it was used at micro locations where specific police units or members of the secretariat happened to be and so on and so forth. The transmission of dispatch was possible and was organized in such a way that it was conveyed via courier. The telephone communications were used, the public communication, the telephone communications service was used from Pristina outwards [as interpreted]. Nothing else was used. Sir, I said that the switchboard in the Pristina SUP building was destroyed, and when we're talking about the equipment that is not wartime equipment but was meant for stationary work conditions, we did not manage to repair the switchboard until the end of the war. Throughout the whole time, it was out of operation, and this applied to some other equipment too. We didn't have an unlimited quantity of equipment. The ministry had a certain limited quantity of equipment at its disposal, and it was being destroyed at quite a rapid rate, so then we reached the point where there was no longer any equipment left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Page 26, line 16, the witness said telephone communications service was used from Pristina outwards towards Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After all this damage to your communications, in addition to using couriers what other means did the MUP use to communicate reporting up to superiors in Serbia and reporting to subordinate units in the field in Kosovo? Was there anything else other than couriers?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that the MUP even before the war had an organized network of transmission and receiver equipment on the KT equipment system. The KT system of communications was not really applied in peacetime conditions because there was no need for that. It was possible using trained radio telegraphers who were trained in the use of these devices, they could also broadcast short written messages as well. But since in the work of these KT broadcasters and receivers there are very powerful broadcasters of 100-plus watts. It's not so easy to use the equipment even the trained professionals using the equipment were concerned about using or being near this equipment because the radiation could simply be detected. So there was panic and fear in case the equipment was switched off. The system could be used to just convey brief messages from one location to another, something that was brief, essential, and possibly very urgent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I may have missed it earlier. Can you explain to me what the KT equipment is and the KT system?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a device that works on the frequency range from 3 to 30 megahertz. The range is called that because the radio waves are the so-called short waves, so it's the short-wave system of communications, Kratki Talasi, KT. So it's a classic device, something that radio -- ham radio operators use, it is very similar equipment to that used by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Short-wave now is a term that I understand. I would like to quickly show you an exhibit, this is P1993. I can give you a hard copy because this is several pages and there's just one point I want to ask you about. This is a meeting dated the 11th of May, 1999, the MUP staff in Pristina, and there's a reference -- I think it's on page 5 of the B/C/S for you. The commander named Colic from the 124th Brigade is speaking, and I think it's the fifth bullet point up from the bottom of his speech, and we're on page 12 of the English, Your Honours. He says: "I gave three USW radio stations to VJ Commander Jelic to use a month ago, and as this is PJP equipment I requested them back but they've not returned the radio stations to date." Are these short-wave radios or what does that USW refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is a so-called radio station that the police called a UKT or it's actually ultra-high frequency. These short-wave system was not acceptable -- accessible to the users, it was only at the secretariat seats and the users who used it were the operators from the communication system, the technicians. This short-wave system that we talked about earlier was not accessible to the police, it was at the seats of the secretariats, and these devices were used by communication workers from the communication departments in the secretariats. We're talking about classical stations, hand-held radios that are used by members of the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So these ultra-high frequency radios that the commander here is mentioning having loaned to the VJ are used in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The very high or the ultra-high frequency, UHF and VHF. These are hand-held radio devices that were used by members of the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I assume if they were loaned to the army, the army and then PJP could talk to each other on them, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, most probably that's the case. I know that the army did not have enough hand-held stations, and this is probably then that cooperation that was organized between the detachments, the companies, and the units of the army in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because of the problems that MUP was having with communications, did you in MUP get any assistance from the VJ in perhaps using some of their equipment or their system, particularly to transmit or communication between Kosovo and Serbia or Pristina and Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, I really did not -- was -- didn't have information about the damage during the war suffered by the Army of Yugoslavia, but I know that a large amount of the equipment was destroyed, so they didn't even have enough for themselves never mind enough to lend to the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Deretic, in your job did you have anything to do with monitoring, intercepting, or eavesdropping on communications of KLA or NATO or any of that kind of thing or was that done by someone else in the DB?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our communications department does not have that within its job description -- well, that we were following this, well, yes, we were because we had to. The KLA members were on our channels more than they were on their own. So in view of all the jamming that was there -- well, yes in that part we did follow it because they were constantly using the radio communications of the ministry both for jamming and for causing certain verbal conflicts and so on and so forth. There were provocations, taunts that were always present on our radio communications. From that point of view, yes, I did follow that mode of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I certainly have no question that your communications system was severely disrupted because of the deliberate bombing of communication networks, but we've seen evidence in this case that, for example, there were several meetings in Pristina of the MUP that included all the SUP chiefs and the PJP commanders. And we've seen some daily reports going from MUP staff up to the ministry which contained information that appeared to be from the previous 24 hours in the hinterlands of Kosovo, which seems to reflect that the information was being communicated. How was that being done? Was it -- was that all via the couriers and hand-held radios?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could not be done through hand-held radios, only via courier. This is certainly information that was of a confidential nature. To use radio networks, I mean I've already said that our radio communications were intercepted, jammed, eavesdropped on, so it was only the most necessary communication that took place via that, but the confidential material was sent via courier. I'm talking about the secretariat in Kosovo and Metohija and communication that went to Pristina. From Pristina and to MUP and to the rest of Serbia, well yes, a fax could be sent, for instance, if nothing else because public communications were operational, telephones too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What about the KT equipment and the KT system, could certain confidential material of an urgent nature be sent via that system?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this equipment was used very rarely, perhaps two or three times, for conveying some very short pieces of information for the reasons I already mentioned. Even I as head of department had a problem to make people who were trained to use that equipment to actually sit and use that equipment because they were afraid of bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say have already given me the answer to this next one where above you said public communication were operational, telephones too. Mr. Joksic from the RDB was here and testified about having provided a telephone to Ibrahim Rugova in his house in Pristina so that he could be in contact with some of the internationals like Mr. Christopher Hill in Skopje and Macedonia. So is it correct that the telephones were still working at least in some parts of Kosovo during the bombing so that you could make calls to outside countries?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you said that Joksic said that? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Mr. Joksic said, that he had ensured that, well the reason was, as far as I can remember, Mr. Rugova had a house somewhere at Dragodan, I don't know the exact locality, but as the Dragodan hill practically within Pristina. That part, that territory was covered by the Telekom organization through the public network. They would install these regional telephone exchanges, that's what they were called, so every region or area was covered with a particular telephone exchange. Vranjevac, Dragodan, other neighbourhoods like that were covered by this telecommunications centre that was in UKT 2. When this cable concentration went down, it was a big problem to make any kind of telephone connection. I assume that Mr. Joksic said that he spoke to the technical teams of Telekom to find some solutions to introduce a public telephone number. They probably did that. I really don't know. And with this kind of number there was communication towards Belgrade or further on through international telephone exchanges to the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The last topic I wanted to deal with was something I think Judge Bonomy asked you about. The PJP detachments I think you told us had only double- or triple-digit numbers or designators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the name of the detachment, its prefix had two or three digits. So the digit's name is the 22nd PJP Detachment. What I'm trying to say is that the number before the detachment designation was a two-digit or a three-digit one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you talking about just during the war in 1999 or do you include the pre-war period in 1999 and 1998 when you say that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all the time. The detachments had the same names, the same designations, the 21st, the 35th, the 36th, as far as I know of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you one last exhibit, this is our Exhibit P1434. With the usher's assistance I'll hand you a hard copy. This is a VJ document dated the 19th of September, 1998, from General Pavkovic, Pristina Corps command. This is an order to support MUP forces in breaking up Siptar terrorists in the Cicavica area. I wanted to have you look at two things. First of all, if you could go to page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is page 8 of the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Under item 5.2 we have a task for the 15th Armoured Brigade. Do you find that, Mr. Deretic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5.2, 15th Armoured Brigade, to support the MUP forces to break-up, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And you'll see about two or three lines down: "The tasks support attack by the 1st PJP Detachment ..." And if you go on to the next heading: "Engage battle group 15.2," its task is to support attack by the 8th PJP Detachment. So we've got a couple of examples there of PJP detachments referred to by single digits. Do you know why General Pavkovic would be doing that, unless there were, indeed, such designators?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of my work and all the obligations I had, I really would not know how to answer this question, why it was marked in this way in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough. If you could go to your page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's page 18 in the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Under the heading command and communications, I've highlighted it in pink there. The second paragraph says: "Arrange communications according to the communications plan to be drawn up by the chief of communications Pristina Corps and the MUP." Now, in this kind of joint action who from the MUP would be involved in arranging communications with the Pristina Corps chief of communications, do you know? This is September 1998.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I did not take part in the elaboration of this communications plan, so I cannot confirm with any certainty who this was. But I can say that PJP detachments had their signals people, their communications people, who knew the organization of radio networks and who knew what radio channels would be used. That could be done by the commander himself. For example, he'd have a chief of communications in the PJP. A communications man is a technician, an experienced engineer, and every PJP had one, and they gave this technical support to every PJP unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, a couple -- a few things after that. First of all, did you know personally the chief of communications for the Pristina Corps in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know -- well, I knew Colonel [Realtime transcript read in error "General"] Mladenovic, who was chief of the stationary communications node. Now, whether he was the chief of communications of the Pristina Corps at the same time, I really don't know. I know that he was in charge of these stationary nodes, that is to say these emission or broadcasting locations where radio networks were organized and where radio equipment was installed and so on and so forth. So I knew three or four men there, him and a few of his associates, and when necessary I spoke to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To save you going through the whole document I would tell you that these tasks for the VJ asked them to support several different MUP units, the 1st, 3rd, 5th, and 8th PJP Detachments, a PJP company from Kosovska Mitrovica, one from Pec, one from Djakovica, also the SAJ and the JSO. Now, who from the MUP would be involved in arranging communications with the VJ when you've got that many diverse and different elements of the MUP involved? Wouldn't it have to be somebody higher than a communications person from one of the PJP detachments, especially since you've got both DB and JB units involved?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps maybe Milan Cankovic who had this technical details [as interpreted], I mean in terms of coverage, maybe he made a suggestion. But at any rate it was about the technical capacities, what radio channels could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Cepic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, it doesn't say that Cankovic was chief of communications, and that is what the witness did mention. We have another mistake in the transcript, page 34, line 19, it's not General Mladenovic, it's Colonel Mladenovic, those were the witness's words. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your point about Cankovic? I'm not following that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think he's saying the witness actually spoke the words "chief of communications" and that wasn't reflected in the transcript. I thought I heard that too, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We note that. Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Deretic, in September 1998 to your knowledge was he then a captain, Captain Cankovic was the chief of communications on the MUP staff, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From mid-1998 when General Lukic was appointed head of staff and Miroslav Mijatovic deputy head of staff, he was on that staff and I think he was there all the way up to the 1st of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question, with regard to code-names or radio code-names, did you ever hear the code-name Brazil associated with the SAJ in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Brazil was the call-sign for the commander of the JSO. Brazil is a call-sign or code sign that was used by the JSO. This was the special unit of the state security sector, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the commander of the JSO you're referring to, is that Milorad Ulemek or Lukovic known as Legija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most probably it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Deretic, are you able to say to what extent the communications systems in Belgrade were damaged by NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to try to remember this. I think it was either the 4th or the 5th of April when the building of the seat of the ministry in Belgrade was destroyed. I know that on that occasion the telecommunications room where the equipment was burned down completely. Of course, in view of the fact that later on I was head of that department, I know full well what was in that communications room in terms of equipment. That's also where the main telephone exchange for the special telephone network was destroyed. So in that way communication was disabled among the secretariats within Serbia, mutual communication, because in the organization of this network -- well, the MUP telephone exchange was the main telephone exchange and all telephone communication went through there. Also in the MUP another exchange was destroyed for transmitting dispatches. So there was serious destruction. Many radio relay facilities that the ministry used in the territory of Serbia, Rudnik, Jastrebac, Crni Vrh, Iriski Venac, all of that was destroyed. So the system of communications at the level of the ministry was also in a state of full collapse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was the ministry's own special network within Serbia restored?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but of course without Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How quickly was that done?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, work is still being done on that. The telephone exchanges are over 30 years old, the ones of the special network. Their GT and Iskra telephone exchanges that were actually inaugurated in 1986 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Deretic, I hope my question was properly translated for you, it was this: Was the ministry's own special network within Serbia restored? And you said: "Yes." And my second question is very simple: How quickly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was only sometime in 2001 that a telephone switchboard was purchased, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So throughout the remainder of the war are you saying that within Serbia itself the MUP's own special network was not restored, there were no communications through it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with a temporary switchboard that was used as a makeshift telephone exchange with a very small number of switches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So my question is: How quickly was that done?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After June 1999 when I came there, this telephone exchange was operational. I don't know when it was installed, this temporary solution with a smaller capacity telephone exchange and switchboard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you would look at an exhibit, please, P1252. I think Mr. Hannis drew your attention to this, and if you look at the ninth person referred to on that is Cankovic, and just take it from me that you're number 10 for the moment because to see that we have to change pages -- in fact, you can go on to the -- just hold it there as it is at the moment. Now, you'll see that this is a decision on the composition of the staff, leaders and members of the staff of the MUP for Kosovo and Metohija. And it's headed up by Major-General Lukic, and it includes you. Now could we go to the second page, where you will see that you are number 10, and you see there that the work was to begin on the 1st of June, 1998, and that the personnel named, including you, were to remain in the staff up to one year, and that's signed by Colonel-General Djordjevic. Now could you look, please, at P1251. Sorry -- yes, just -- this is my mistake, I'm sorry about this. Could we just go back to page 2 of 1252, it's still on in English. Could we go back also to the Serb. Page 2, please. Can you read the date of that document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a 098.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I think there's an 11, but the month is missing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the month either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I want you to -- we need to have a break now, and I'd like you to hold that information in your head and we'll come back to look at something else after the break. Could you now leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will see you again at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Deretic, could you now look at P1251. Now, you'll see that's a decision on the formation of a staff of the ministry in Pristina, and you'll see in paragraph 2 the task of the staff is to plan, organize, guide, and coordinate the work of the secretariats of the interior and the border police station in performing complex and important duties and assignments. And then the subject matter of these assignments is set out, and if you go to paragraph 4, you'll see that it provides that the composition of the staff, the leader and members of the staff, will be laid down in a separate decision. And this one is also signed by Djordjevic and is dated the 15th of May, 1998. And you will remember that the previous one identified General Lukic as the staff leader and Djinovic as the deputy leader and various other people as leaders for particular subjects, including you as assistant head of staff for wire communications. Now, can you tell me what that body -- or whether you were in the position set out in these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Friday I said that I saw this document for the first time during proofing, the lawyers showed it to me. I had not seen that document ever before nor had it ever been handed to me. All the time until the 1st of June I was chief of communications in Pristina, and in keeping with my purview and the rules defining our duties and responsibilities I performed my work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And remind me, where was Cankovic during that period?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cankovic was part of the staff, he was on the staff as chief of communications on the staff led by Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what were your dealings with him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I performed regular work on the maintenance and operation of the system of communications. In my work I was answerable to the chief of secretariat and the line administration within the ministry. I was in contact with Cankovic when some equipment needed to be reinforced or batteries had to be provided. In that situation when there were problems with power facing various police units, I would request that equipment to be supplied for various reasons. It is the ministry that deals with supplies of equipment, namely, the administration for communications, and it distributes this equipment to various units. So that was the nature of our contacts. We reviewed various needs and requirements, requests had to be made to the administration for communications within the ministry, and that was our tactical logistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How regularly were you in communication with him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't say that we were regularly in contact; contacts were sporadic. I couldn't say now whether it was two or three times or five times because the communications department was doing its job under Article 45. Our job was to check on a daily basis how the system was operating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In what period of time do you say you were in contact with him between two and five times?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, within a month, 30 days, but I couldn't really say precisely because those were not real meetings. He would drop by my office. It was not a formal meeting. He would just point out a problem in the operation of the system of communications or tell me that some back-up equipment needed to be supplied such as batteries for vehicle-mounted or hand-held stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You only need to answer the question I actually ask you, Mr. Deretic. Now, can you confirm to me that all the persons who were on the -- who were named on the decision that I showed you were members of the public security branch of the MUP or do you need to see it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a hard copy if that will assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please, if you could give him --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You want just 1252 for now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 1252 for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a simple yes or no. Are they all members of the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now would you look, please, at P1505. Now, you'll see that this is dated the 16th of June, 1998, and is said to be a decision to establish a ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism, remarkably similar title to what we have just been looking at. You're not named this time, but you'll see that on the first page Cankovic's name is there. Now, if we can go just quickly to the second page so that you can see the signature, and you'll see this time it's signed by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the minister of course had authority over both the state security and the public security sectors?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And at that time the state security sector was within the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Unlike the authority of Djordjevic, which extended only to the public security sector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the chief of sector led the work of the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but Djordjevic's responsibilities were confined to public security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. The chief of sector, public security, leads the work of organizational units within that sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's go back to the first page of this order or decision, rather. And just look at the names and tell me if it's fair to say that they are a mixture of personnel from the state security sector and the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that two members belonged to the state security, that is to say they were not members of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And which two are they?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: David Gajic and Milorad Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then if you go down to the end of the names and you'll see a reference to the expanded staff and that was to include chiefs of the SUPs and also chiefs of the branches of the RDB; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written here, but I have to stress again that I saw this for the first time during proofing so I didn't know whether these people from the state security were really on the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just please deal with the questions I ask you, Mr. Deretic. And these also are a mixture of personnel from the public security sector and personnel from the state security sector?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these two are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, would you go now to paragraph 6 which is on the second page, and do we see there that among the orders or decisions that are superseded by this one, are the two documents that you looked at earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that this one from 11th of June, 1996 is among them. I didn't remember the date of the other document you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it may be the translation that's given us the wrong -- it's the 11th of June, 1998, and that's the document on which you could see the 11 and the 1998 but you couldn't see the month, if you remember. And it also involves the recall of the one of the 15th of May which you say. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It is indeed 1998.

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this document I have in my hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I recall from you on these matters. Mr. Ivetic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Why don't we start from the back and work our way forwards. Mr. Deretic, Judge Bonomy asked you about the significance of the signature of Minister Stojiljkovic. If we could have up again P1811, that was the document from May 31st, 1999, by which you did become a member of the MUP staff for Pristina and also signed by Minister Stojiljkovic himself. The named persons in that document here we have the first page and there are four more on the second page, if you could take a look at these and when you're finished with the names on the first page if you could tell us so that we can have the second page displayed to you. And the question I have for you, sir, looking at these named individuals who are named to the MUP staff, are any of these RDB personnel or are they exclusively RJB?

utterances.speaker: MILOS DERETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're all from public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
